text:
The headline number, 72% of customers satisfied, can mislead.

The survey was emailed to 40,000 people, and 1,000 of them chose to respond. That means it measures who was willing to answer, not how satisfied customers are.

Falling response rates make this worse. Pew's telephone response rate dropped from 36% in 1997 to 6% by 2018. As fewer people respond, the sample tilts toward people with strong feelings, either delighted or furious.

The report also quotes a margin of error of ±3 points. That figure assumes the respondents were chosen at random, and they were not. It accounts for ordinary sampling noise but ignores the bias from self-selection.

History offers a warning. In 1936, the Literary Digest collected 2.4 million returned ballots, far more than any competitor. It confidently picked Landon, yet Roosevelt carried 46 states.

Analysts should assume the number flatters the survey's sponsor. They should trust it only after weighting the data against census benchmarks shows it holds up.
